title: Respiratory Histology
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the airway wall from the trachea to the alveolus and explains why its lining, cartilage, glands, and muscle change at each level. It covers the cells that clean the air, the cells that exchange gas and repair the alveolus, the ciliary machinery of mucociliary clearance, the blood-air barrier, and the squamous lining of the true vocal folds. Board questions use this histology to explain smoking injury, primary ciliary dyskinesia, air trapping in emphysema, low diffusing capacity in fibrosis and edema, and the predominance of squamous cell carcinoma in the larynx.
prerequisites: Classification of epithelia by layering and cell shape, and the basement membrane
Microtubules, motor proteins (dynein), and ATP hydrolysis
Gross anatomy of the larynx, trachea, and bronchial tree (PU-3, PU-4)
Lung bud development and surfactant maturation (PU-1)
Metaplasia, dysplasia, and neoplasia as general pathology concepts

connections.how: Surfactant from type II cells and alveolar tethering of bronchioles determine compliance, airway resistance, and expiratory airway collapse.
The thickness and area of the blood-air barrier enter directly into Fick's law and the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
Dynein gene mutations cause primary ciliary dyskinesia, and CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis, two different routes to failed mucus clearance.
Chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and interstitial fibrosis are each explained by injury to a specific layer or cell described here.
Squamous metaplasia in smokers and the native squamous lining of the vocal folds explain where squamous cell carcinoma arises.

terms.def: A single layer of cells that all touch the basement membrane but whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks layered.
A mucus-secreting epithelial cell whose apical cytoplasm is filled with mucinogen granules.
A nonciliated, dome-topped secretory cell of the bronchioles that makes protective proteins, metabolizes inhaled chemicals, and serves as a local progenitor (formerly called the Clara cell).
A very thin squamous alveolar cell that covers most of the alveolar surface and forms the epithelial part of the blood-air barrier.
A cuboidal alveolar cell with lamellar bodies that secretes surfactant and divides to replace injured type I cells.
A membrane-bound organelle in type II cells that stores surfactant phospholipid in concentric layers before secretion.
The microtubule core of a cilium, arranged as nine outer doublets around a central pair (9 plus 2).
The outward pull that elastic alveolar walls exert on the bronchioles embedded among them, holding the bronchioles open.
Reversible replacement of ciliated columnar epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium in response to chronic irritation.
The tissue gas crosses between alveolar air and capillary blood: type I cell, fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium.
Diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide, a measure of how readily gas crosses the blood-air barrier, which falls when the barrier thickens or its area is lost.

sections.title: How the airway epithelium changes from trachea to alveolus

blocks.text: The conducting airways warm, humidify, and clean inspired air, while the respiratory portion exchanges gas. The lining changes along the tree to match these jobs, and it does so gradually rather than at sharp boundaries. As a rule, the epithelium becomes shorter and simpler distally, goblet cells thin out, and ciliated cells give way to secretory club cells and finally to the flat cells of the alveolus.

The trachea and bronchi are lined by respiratory epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Every cell touches the basement membrane, but basal cells (the stem cells of this lining) stay short, so the nuclei sit at several levels. Ciliated cells are the most numerous; goblet cells and the submucosal glands supply the mucus that traps particles. Scattered brush cells and neuroendocrine cells are also present.

In the bronchioles the epithelium becomes simple ciliated columnar, then simple cuboidal in the terminal bronchioles, the last purely conducting segment. Goblet cells fall away and are absent from terminal bronchioles, where club cells take over secretion. Respiratory bronchioles keep a low cuboidal lining with club cells and a few ciliated cells, but alveoli open from their walls, so gas exchange begins at this level. Alveolar ducts, sacs, and alveoli are lined by type I and type II pneumocytes.

blocks.text: This gradient explains where disease appears. Goblet cell hyperplasia and gland enlargement in chronic bronchitis mainly affect the large airways, while centriacinar emphysema in smokers begins at the respiratory bronchiole, the junction of conducting and exchanging tissue. Because the alveolar lining is so thin, injury there leads directly to impaired diffusion and leak of fluid into airspaces.

sections.title: Bronchi versus bronchioles: cartilage, glands, and what holds small airways open

blocks.text: The trachea is held open by 16 to 20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage whose open ends face posteriorly and are bridged by the trachealis smooth muscle. As the trachea divides, the rings give way to irregular cartilage plates in the bronchi. Bronchi also carry seromucous glands in the submucosa, abundant goblet cells, and spirally arranged bundles of smooth muscle in the lamina propria, inside the cartilage.

Bronchioles are defined histologically by the absence of cartilage and submucosal glands. They are usually about 1 mm or less in diameter, goblet cells are few and then absent, and the smooth muscle layer is relatively thick for the size of the tube. A practical rule for slides is that cartilage and glands occur together: where the cartilage plates end, the glands end too.

blocks.title: Bronchus versus bronchiole
rows: Spiral bundles in the lamina propria, inside the cartilage
blocks.caption: Absence of cartilage and glands identifies a bronchiole and explains why its diameter can change.

blocks.text: Without cartilage, a bronchiole's diameter is set by two opposing influences. Smooth muscle tone narrows it; parasympathetic (vagal, muscarinic) activity and mediators such as histamine and leukotrienes increase tone, while beta-2 adrenergic stimulation relaxes it. Radial traction holds it open: bronchioles run through the lung parenchyma, and the elastic walls of the surrounding alveoli attach to their outer surface and pull outward. That pull increases as lung volume increases, which is why airway resistance falls at high lung volumes.

blocks.title: Loss of radial traction in emphysema
steps: Protease destruction of alveolar walls
Fewer elastic attachments pull on each bronchiole
Forced expiration raises pleural pressure around small airways
Unsupported bronchioles collapse early in expiration
Air is trapped distally; residual volume rises
blocks.caption: Emphysema narrows small airways by removing their external support, not by thickening their walls.

blocks.text: This explains two classic patterns. In asthma, smooth muscle contraction narrows both bronchi and bronchioles, but bronchioles narrow most freely because no cartilage limits them. In emphysema, the bronchiole wall may be nearly normal, but loss of tethering lets it close during forced expiration, producing air trapping and an increased residual volume. Cartilage protects the bronchi from this expiratory collapse, so air trapping arises in the small airways.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient with emphysema have more trouble breathing out forcefully than breathing in?
blocks.explain: During inspiration pleural pressure is negative and pulls bronchioles open, while during forced expiration positive pleural pressure squeezes bronchioles that have lost the alveolar attachments that normally hold them open.

sections.title: Type I and type II pneumocytes, club cells, and alveolar macrophages

blocks.text: Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous cells that cover about 95% of the alveolar surface, although they make up only about 40% of alveolar epithelial cells. Their cytoplasm spreads into sheets thin enough for gas to cross easily, and tight junctions between them stop fluid leaking from the interstitium into the airspace. They do not divide and are easily injured by toxins, oxidants, and infection.

Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells that bulge into the alveolus, often at the corners where alveolar walls meet. They are more numerous than type I cells but cover only about 5% of the surface. Their lamellar bodies store surfactant, a mixture of phospholipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and surfactant proteins A, B, C, and D. Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension, which increases compliance and keeps small alveoli from collapsing. Proteins A and D also bind microbes and help macrophages engulf them. Type II cells are the progenitors of the alveolus: after injury they proliferate and differentiate into new type I cells, so type II cell hyperplasia on biopsy is a sign of alveolar damage and repair.

Club cells are nonciliated cells with dome-shaped apices that project into the lumen of bronchioles, most densely in terminal bronchioles. They secrete club cell secretory protein and other protective proteins into the fluid lining the small airways. Their abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum contains cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize inhaled chemicals; this can detoxify a compound or convert it into a reactive product, so club cells are both protectors and targets. They also act as progenitors that renew themselves and ciliated cells after bronchiolar injury.

Alveolar macrophages lie on the alveolar surface and in the septa. They are derived from monocytes: most arise from fetal monocytes that seed the lung around birth and then renew locally, and blood monocytes add to them during inflammation. They phagocytose particles, microbes, and surplus surfactant, then move up the mucociliary escalator or enter lymphatics. Macrophages filled with carbon are called dust cells. In chronic left heart failure, red cells leak from congested alveolar capillaries, macrophages break down their hemoglobin, and the iron is stored as hemosiderin; these hemosiderin-laden macrophages, called heart failure cells, stain blue with Prussian blue and point to chronic pulmonary congestion.

sections.title: Mucociliary clearance, the ciliary axoneme, and how clearance fails

blocks.text: Mucociliary clearance is the main defense of the conducting airways. The surface fluid has two layers: a thin, watery periciliary layer in which the cilia beat freely, and a gel mucus layer on top that traps inhaled particles and microbes. Each ciliated cell carries about 200 to 300 cilia that beat in coordinated waves; the tips catch the mucus during the forward stroke and carry the blanket upward toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. Clearance needs three things: working cilia, mucus of the right amount and viscosity, and enough periciliary fluid, whose depth depends on ion transport through channels such as CFTR.

Each motile cilium is built around an axoneme of nine outer microtubule doublets surrounding two central single microtubules, the 9 plus 2 pattern. Inner and outer dynein arms project from each doublet toward its neighbor. Dynein is an ATPase motor: it hydrolyzes ATP and walks along the adjacent doublet, so neighboring doublets try to slide past each other. Nexin links and radial spokes tie the doublets together and to the central pair, so that sliding cannot run freely and is converted into bending. The cilium grows from a basal body of nine microtubule triplets with no central pair.

blocks.title: Mucociliary clearance
steps: Inhaled particles stick to mucus from goblet cells and glands
Dynein arms hydrolyze ATP and slide adjacent outer doublets
Nexin links and radial spokes convert sliding into bending
Coordinated beats move the mucus blanket toward the pharynx
Mucus is swallowed or coughed out
blocks.caption: Clearance fails if cilia stop, mucus becomes abnormal, or the periciliary fluid layer is lost.

blocks.text: Smoking damages clearance from both sides. Smoke slows ciliary beating, and chronic irritation stimulates goblet cell hyperplasia and enlargement of submucosal glands, so more mucus is made. With persistent injury, basal cells differentiate into stratified squamous epithelium instead of ciliated columnar cells. This squamous metaplasia is an adaptation: the new lining resists irritation but has no cilia and no goblet cells, so in metaplastic patches the escalator stops. Metaplasia is reversible if smoking stops, but under continued exposure it can progress to dysplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus.

blocks.title: Smoking and loss of airway clearance
steps: Smoke chronically irritates the bronchial lining
Glands enlarge and goblet cells multiply: more mucus
Cilia slow and squamous metaplasia removes ciliated cells
Mucus is made faster than it is cleared and pools
Bacteria grow in retained mucus: recurrent bronchitis and pneumonia
blocks.caption: Increased production plus reduced removal is the mechanism of chronic productive cough and infection in smokers.

blocks.text: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is an autosomal recessive defect of ciliary structure, most often absent or abnormal dynein arms. Mucus is normal, but cilia cannot move it, so patients have chronic sinusitis, otitis, and bronchiectasis from repeated infection. The same motor drives sperm flagella, so men are usually infertile, and motile cilia in the embryonic node set left-right asymmetry, so about half of patients have situs inversus. The triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis is called Kartagener syndrome.

blocks.title: Worked example: two causes of retained mucus
blocks.text: A 20-year-old has recurrent pneumonia, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Step 1: ask whether the problem is the mucus or the cilia. In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR reduces chloride and fluid secretion, the periciliary layer collapses, and thick mucus pins down cilia that are themselves normal; pancreatic insufficiency and a high sweat chloride follow from the same channel defect in other organs. Step 2: in primary ciliary dyskinesia, the mucus is normal but the axoneme lacks working dynein arms, so cilia are immotile or beat abnormally. Step 3: look for clues outside the lung. Dextrocardia or male infertility with immotile sperm points to ciliary dyskinesia; steatorrhea and salty sweat point to cystic fibrosis.

Oxygen moving from alveolar gas into blood crosses the blood-air barrier. On the thin side of each alveolar septum, the barrier has three tissue layers: the cytoplasm of a type I pneumocyte, the fused basement membranes of the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium, and the capillary endothelial cell. Gas also passes through the thin surfactant-containing fluid film on the alveolar surface and, after the endothelium, through plasma and the red cell membrane. Over most of its area the barrier is about 0.2 to 0.6 micrometers thick, and its total area in an adult is about 70 square meters.

blocks.title: Path of oxygen from alveolus to hemoglobin
steps: Alveolar gas
Surface fluid film with surfactant
Type I pneumocyte cytoplasm
Fused basement membranes
Capillary endothelium
Plasma, red cell membrane, hemoglobin
blocks.caption: Thickening at any step lengthens the diffusion path.

blocks.text: Each septum also has a thick side, where the basement membranes separate around an interstitium of fibroblasts, collagen, and elastic fibers. Alveolar walls themselves lack lymphatics; interstitial fluid moves toward lymphatics that begin around the smallest bronchioles and vessels. Excess filtered fluid collects first on the thick side, which protects gas exchange early, but fluid that exceeds lymphatic drainage widens the barrier and then floods alveoli.

Fick's law states that the rate of gas transfer across a sheet of tissue is proportional to its area, the partial pressure difference, and the diffusion constant of the gas, and inversely proportional to its thickness. Thickening the barrier therefore slows transfer. In interstitial fibrosis, repeated injury to type I cells is followed by type II cell hyperplasia, fibroblast proliferation, and collagen deposition in the septa. In interstitial edema, fluid widens the interstitium. Both lower DLCO. Emphysema also lowers DLCO, but by destroying surface area rather than by thickening the barrier.

Oxygen is affected more than carbon dioxide. CO2 is much more soluble and diffuses about 20 times faster across the barrier, so it still equilibrates when O2 transfer has become limited. At rest, red cells spend about 0.75 s in the alveolar capillary, while O2 normally equilibrates within about 0.25 s, leaving a large reserve. A thickened barrier uses up part of that reserve, so resting saturation may be near normal. During exercise, transit time can fall to about 0.25 s, equilibration is no longer complete, and saturation falls.

blocks.title: Worked example: why fibrosis shows first with exertion
blocks.text: A patient with interstitial fibrosis has a barrier about twice normal thickness. Step 1: by Fick's law, doubling thickness at the same gradient halves the rate of O2 transfer, so equilibration takes roughly twice as long, about 0.5 s instead of 0.25 s. Step 2: at rest, transit time is about 0.75 s, so blood still nearly equilibrates and saturation is close to normal. Step 3: with exercise, transit falls toward 0.25 s, blood leaves before equilibrating, and the patient desaturates. Step 4: PaCO2 is normal or low, because CO2 diffuses easily and the patient hyperventilates. In practice, resting hypoxemia in fibrosis also reflects ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

blocks.predict: Why does a thickened blood-air barrier lower PaO2 with exercise but leave PaCO2 normal or low?
blocks.explain: Exercise shortens capillary transit time below what slowed O2 diffusion needs, while CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster and the hypoxemia drives extra ventilation that removes CO2.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on transit time and the worked example in this section.

sections.title: Stratified squamous epithelium of the true vocal folds and oropharynx, and laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma

blocks.text: Not every surface of the upper airway carries respiratory epithelium. Where friction or abrasion is constant, the lining is nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium: many cell layers, with the surface cells flattened and still nucleated. This covers the oropharynx and laryngopharynx, which carry swallowed food, the lingual surface and upper laryngeal surface of the epiglottis, and the true vocal folds, whose surfaces strike each other hundreds of times per second during speech. Stratified squamous epithelium withstands this wear but has no cilia, so clearance across it relies on swallowing and coughing.

The true vocal fold has, beneath its epithelium, a loose superficial lamina propria (Reinke space) that lets the mucosa ripple over the deeper vocal ligament and the vocalis muscle. The false vocal folds (vestibular folds) above them, the lower laryngeal surface of the epiglottis, and the larynx below the folds have respiratory epithelium. The nasopharynx is mainly respiratory epithelium, with some stratified squamous areas.

blocks.title: Linings of the upper airway
rows: Epiglottis, lingual and upper laryngeal surfaces
blocks.caption: Squamous linings mark sites of mechanical stress; respiratory epithelium marks conducting surfaces that need clearance.

blocks.text: About 95% of malignant laryngeal tumors are squamous cell carcinomas. They arise from the native squamous epithelium of the true folds, and from squamous metaplasia elsewhere in the larynx, through a sequence driven mainly by tobacco smoke, with alcohol acting synergistically. Histologically they show keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, the features of squamous differentiation.

blocks.title: Progression to laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
steps: Chronic tobacco and alcohol exposure
Squamous hyperplasia and keratosis (white plaque, leukoplakia)
Dysplasia of increasing grade
Carcinoma in situ
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma
blocks.caption: Each step reflects accumulating genetic damage in squamous epithelium; the early steps are potentially reversible.

blocks.text: Location shapes the presentation. Glottic tumors on the true folds are the most common and cause hoarseness early, because even a small lesion disrupts vibration; the true folds have few lymphatics, so nodal spread is late. Supraglottic tumors have a rich lymphatic supply and often present with nodal metastases. The oropharynx has the same squamous lining, but there, especially in the tonsils and base of tongue, high-risk human papillomavirus (mainly HPV-16) causes a large share of squamous carcinomas. In the larynx HPV-6 and HPV-11 instead cause benign squamous papillomas, not the usual carcinoma.

blocks.predict: Why does a small carcinoma of the true vocal fold usually present earlier and with fewer nodal metastases than a supraglottic tumor of the same size?
blocks.explain: Any mass on the true fold disturbs vibration and causes hoarseness at once, and the true folds have sparse lymphatic drainage, while the supraglottis is clinically silent longer and drains through a rich lymphatic network.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on location and presentation.

integration.text: Histology links the respiratory chapters. Embryology explains the pattern: the epithelium of the larynx, trachea, and lungs comes from endoderm of the foregut, while cartilage, muscle, and connective tissue come from surrounding mesoderm, and type II cells mature late in fetal life, so preterm infants lack surfactant. Physiology reads the same structures quantitatively: surfactant sets compliance, radial traction sets small airway resistance and the volume dependence of airflow, and barrier thickness and area set DLCO. Genetics and immunology add mechanisms of failure, such as dynein and CFTR mutations and the collectin function of surfactant proteins A and D.

Pathology follows from cell biology. Each cell type has a characteristic injury: ciliated columnar cells undergo squamous metaplasia, goblet cells and glands enlarge in chronic bronchitis, type I cells die in diffuse alveolar damage while type II cells repair, alveolar walls are lost in emphysema, and septa thicken in fibrosis and edema. The limits are worth stating: transitions along the airway are gradual, cell proportions and dimensions vary between sources and species, and impaired gas exchange in most diseases reflects several mechanisms at once rather than barrier thickness alone.

summary: The airway lining flattens distally: pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells in trachea and bronchi, simple cuboidal with club cells in terminal bronchioles, and type I and type II pneumocytes in alveoli.
Bronchi have cartilage plates, submucosal glands, and goblet cells; bronchioles have none of these and prominent smooth muscle.
Bronchioles stay open through the balance of muscle tone and radial traction from alveolar walls; loss of that traction in emphysema causes expiratory collapse and air trapping.
Type I pneumocytes cover about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange but cannot divide; type II cells secrete surfactant and regenerate type I cells.

Club cells secrete protective proteins, metabolize inhaled chemicals with cytochrome P450, and act as bronchiolar progenitors; alveolar macrophages clear particles and become heart failure cells in chronic congestion.
Cilia have a 9 plus 2 axoneme; dynein ATPase slides doublets and nexin links convert sliding to bending, moving mucus toward the pharynx.
Smoking increases mucus while squamous metaplasia removes cilia, so mucus pools and infections recur; dynein defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus in about half.
The blood-air barrier is type I cell, fused basement membranes, and endothelium; fibrosis or edema thickens it, lowers DLCO, and causes desaturation first with exercise.
True vocal folds and oropharynx have nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and about 95% of laryngeal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas linked to tobacco and alcohol.

verify: Bronchiole diameter is given as about 1 mm or less in most sources, but Junqueira describes intralobular airways of up to about 5 mm as bronchioles; confirm the cutoff NABNE expects.
Proportions of alveolar cells vary between sources: type I cells cover about 95% to 97% of the surface and make up about 40% of alveolar epithelial cells; type II cells cover about 3% to 5%.
Blood-air barrier thickness (about 0.2 to 0.6 micrometers) and alveolar surface area (quoted from about 50 to 100 square meters, Guyton and Hall about 70) vary by source and method.
Capillary transit time (about 0.75 s at rest, about 0.25 s in heavy exercise) and O2 equilibration time (about 0.25 s) are consensus approximations; some texts give a resting transit time of 0.8 s.

Alveolar macrophage origin: review books state derivation from blood monocytes, while current immunology shows most resident alveolar macrophages arise from fetal monocytes and self-renew; confirm the expected answer.
Number of tracheal cartilage rings (16 to 20) and cilia per ciliated cell (about 200 to 300) are approximate and differ slightly between texts.
The share of laryngeal malignancies that are squamous cell carcinoma is given as about 95% in Robbins; some sources quote over 90%.
Confirm whether NABNE uses the current term club cell, the older eponym Clara cell, or both.
